subject: Widely distributed species dragging results for deeper nodes?

messages.author: ef13d6499a420f45
messages.subject: Widely distributed species dragging results for deeper nodes?
parts:
Dear BGBears,
By adapting the Psychotria example, I successfully (!) used
BioGeoBEARS to infer ancestral distributions of a lizard genus. DECj
was found to be the winner among the 6 models implemented
out-of-the-box by the package, based on a range of pairwise likelihood
tests and AICs.

I have a concern, though.

In my dataset, I have a single species that occurs in 4 areas (all
others occur in 1). Resulting ranges for deeper nodes correspond to
this species' distribution. It seems that this single, widespread
species is driving the reconstruction of all nodes ancestral to it.

I assume that this is an effect of not including outgroups in my
analyses. Because related genera diverged too long ago and have too
wide distributions, I assumed they would hardly be informative.

Does it make sense that the widespread species may be shaping results
for the deeper nodes? Should I include outgroups anyway?

Thanks! Ivan.

messages.author: 665b3d97beb30882
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Widely distributed species dragging results for deeper nodes?
parts:
Hi Ivan,

The behavior you describe is not necessarily unexpected under DEC-type models.  There are 3 cladogenesis processes in DEC:

format: ancestor range -> left range, right range

1. sympatry, e.g. A -> A,A

2. subset sympatry, e.g. ABCD -> A, ABCD

3. narrow vicariance, e.g.: ABCD -> A, BCD


For widespread ancestors, there are more possible #2-type events than the others, see:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/biogeobears/kmbkmfXzGSg

...especially:

https://googledrive.com/host/0B6HJElw5txrwZlhjQ0ZUcEdzUG8/ch2_SuppData_01_cladogenesis_parameterizations_v03.xlsx

...so #2 events often get a lot of the probability.  This would mean if you have a sister pair of species:

sp1: A
sp2: ABCD

...the ancestor will be ABCD with high probability.  If THEIR sister is also A (or B or some other single-area range), then the next ancestor can also be ABCD.  This can hypothetically continue all the way to the root, although the probabilities will probably get more spread out.

DEC+J won't necessarily change this, especially for low-ish values of j, since DEC+J still contains all of the DEC processes.

This scenario would suggest that a widespread species evolved long ago and as it continued to evolve through time, it continually threw off narrow-range endemic sister lineages.  Which actually might be a reasonable idea in some situations, e.g. there are widespread flying bird species that have various flightless species on remote islands, and this has happened recently enough that some of the flightless species still nest within the large-population flying species.

If one doesn't like this reconstruction, there are various options such as fixing/eliminating certain ranges at some ancestral nodes, limiting the maximum range size, etc., but most of these would probably lower the likelihood.  Time-stratified analyses might rule out certain ranges at certain time periods also...

Cheers!
Nick
